utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we hear the witness, there are three matters that we have to deal with. Oh, I'm very glad Ms. Chana is present in this courtroom. Frankly speaking, we miss you very much since there's some motions that we have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- deal with. The first issue is that the Defence counsel will furnish us with some information about the chain of custody of the documents yesterday we used. The second issue is about the petition of the Prosecution concerning the document of the, I think, MFI108. The third issue is about the protective measures for the next witness. Let's go through them one by one. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. As requested last night by Your Honour, we have made a few inquiries about the chain of custody of that document and we believe of the Chamber present today in Court is our investigator, Mr. Asim Dzambasovic, who is the person who located that document. That document, as mentioned yesterday, I believe, was found in the military archives of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo. The Defence put an official request to the Ministry of Defence to obtain that document. Unfortunately, the request that we put is in Sarajevo, but we've made a number of phone calls late last night to be faxed our request together with the official response from the ministry, as they provided us with that document, and we hope to be receiving that fax in the course of the morning. For the time being, what we have, Your Honour, is the actual pages of the log which we obtained from the archives. It is this document. The first page is not part of the document. Instead -- in the sense it's a cover page which has been written by an investigator. However, the rest of the document contains it is photocopies made for the Defence by the archives of the 1st Corps, and it's made of three different parts, depending on the names of the former members of the 9th Brigade. It goes into alphabetic order. And for each section there is an official stamp with the signature of the officer who signed the log in question. It has the official stamp of the Bosnian army in three different parts of the document, which we have obtained, including the part which concern Mr. Sakrak himself. As I noted earlier, we are expecting to receive this day our request to the ministry concerning that very document as well as the official response of the ministry or the -- the archive in that respect and we hope to be able to provide those to the Chamber if so required. In addition, we have asked our investigator to be present in court in case Your Honour wanted to ask him any further question as to the whereabouts of those documents, and his having found them in the archives of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re, is that information satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not -- unfortunately, not yet. This is, as far as we -- I don't dispute anything Mr. Mettraux says, but it is information provided from the bar table. At the moment, there are a number of unresolved issues relating to a Defence challenge to the Prosecution's attempt to do exactly the same thing, which is to provide fairly similar information about how we obtained documents, that is, by putting in requests through the Bosnian -- a request for assistance through the Bosnian Embassy here, going to archives in Sarajevo, investigators physically taking documents from them. So I would ask the Court to defer the tender of those sorts of documents until the issue is resolved as to how the Prosecution is allowed to tender its documents and what the Trial Chamber requires us to prove as to the source of the documents or the chain of custody. I mean, on their face, they appear to be the similar sorts of documents. They have one which they say comes from an archive; we have documents we say comes from an archive. And our position is it can't be good enough for the -- it's not fair, the principle of the equality of arms, for the Defence to say -- assert from the bar table, "This is where ours come from," but we're not allowed to do so. There's also another issue on the equality of arms, and that is the Defence has had almost all of our documents for a long time. We don't see these documents, and the first time we saw this document was yesterday, when it was flashed across the screen in front of us. We don't -- we haven't seen the original. And the Prosecution is in an extreme disadvantage in trying to rebut on the spot any -- any issues relating to the provenance of the documents because we have not had time. We see them briefly in court. And finally, on the admissibility of that particular document - this may well resolve the issue on this particular one - our objection is also to the relevance of putting this particular document into evidence now. The witness gave evidence yesterday that he joined -- he became a member of the 9th Motorised Brigade in September, a few days before he went to Herzegovina, Grabovica. He gave that evidence in examination-in-chief and then in cross-examination, and my learned friend showed him a document which he -- which apparently purports to say that he was formally noted for the records of, I assume, the ABiH as having formally joined in November, but his -- his oral evidence is that he was in the brigade from September. And I don't think there's any dispute between the parties that he was in the brigade in September and he went to Grabovica as part of the 9th Mountain Brigade. So in that sense, the tender of this document won't -- won't assist the Trial Chamber in its determination, won't advance the proceedings, and in our view just clutters up the trial record by putting in unnecessary written material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I think the reason you said is just a reason for the relevance of this document in this particular case. I believe that the Defence team is entitled to show any documents to challenge the evidence presented in the direct examination, and we believe that we are satisfied with the reasons at this stage for the chain of custody of that document, and we believe that this document is relevant to -- to this case and the reliability is prima facie satisfied. So we decided to admit it into the evidence, and this rule will apply equally to both parties in the future. And in the future, if there's any new information which disputes the authenticity of this document, any party will be free to inform the Trial Chamber. We could easily reconsider the admission of that document. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In relation to this issue, there is another matter which my colleague from the Prosecution has raised, which is that there are at least three letters from the Defence to the Prosecution in relation to the chain of custody of Prosecution documents. Those letters have been outstanding for months for some of them, and we had been given several undertakings that this information would be provided to the Defence. The Defence will challenge the authenticity of a number of documents. In addition, one of the reasons why the Defence had requested search information relates to the next document which we are going to discuss, the order of the 30th of August, and the realisation on the part of the Defence that something very strange had happened with that document. That triggered our request. And as I just pointed out, those requests for the chain of custody of a number of Prosecution documents are still outstanding and we would really need that information before we can decide whether or not to challenge the authenticity of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I'll respond to this. What had happened, and Mr. Guenael is quite right, is there were some letters that had requested the chain of custody of certain documents. What we had done, Your Honour - and this was at least some, I believe, two and a half months ago; I will stand corrected by the Defence - we had given them the source of all the documents. So for each document on our exhibit list, we'd given them a chart with all the source of documents. Subsequently, Mr. Guenael had sent a letter specifying certain documents, and we are looking into the chain of custody into the specific documents. But I will say one thing here, that some of the documents which are in that list are open-source documents. They are like decrees and statutes and laws, so -- which really begs to question, Your Honour, how seriously have they sort of looked at their own list. Because it's a huge number that they request the chain of custody from. I would request the Defence through Your Honours if they could look at that list again and perhaps take out some of these open-source documents and really leave in the list only those that they truly need to know the chain of custody about. But nevertheless, at this very moment there is somebody being tasked to look at the chain of custody of the documents, and we are not going to give the -- the chain of custody on open documents. We will give them on the others. And a lot of them, Your Honour, are from our collections, very much like the document which has been produced by the Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. On that issue, I agree with you that open documents should not be asked for the chain of custody of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We -- we agree with Your Honour. And if there is indeed search documents on our list, we will definitely take them out and streamline the list. But we have done so already. And this was our understanding, that none of those documents remain on the last letter which we had sent to the Prosecution. But if we are wrong about this, we would certainly undertake to take those open-source documents away from our list and ask the Prosecution to accelerate their research in relation to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's come to the second issue. It's about the position of the Prosecution concerning of the document 108. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position in this -- on this particular document is that we have this memorandum to yourselves, to the Bench, from Philip Hepburn where he actually gives what is he thinks is the definitive translation. Both translations, Your Honour, were done by CLSS. And there is this -- this note which attempts to explain as to why it came about that there are two different meanings. We would, with your leave, Your Honour, request that we would accept the -- the last one, as they say, as a definitive version but we would tender -- would like to tender this -- this memorandum as an exhibit to be attached to that document. I think that probably would be the most expedient way of dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for your cooperation. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Insofar as the issue of the translation is concerned, the Defence would have no problem with the latest version, as confirmed by CLSS, to go in the record and, if necessary, together with that letter. But with respect, we think that the issue here is much more fundamental than a mere issue of translation. I would just point out the two issues which we think are at issue here: The first one relates to the original document; that is the one which was shown to be, let's say, incorrect. The second issue is the swapping of this first document to the second. And I will just touch upon the issue at first. But the original document which contains the word "command" rather than "control" or "direct" and which also misses a crucial sentence as to the nature of the task of the inspection team, was the document which was before Judge Wald, who confirmed the indictment, among other things. This is also the document which was shown to a number of Prosecution witnesses, including their military expert, giving, the Defence submit, an inappropriate impression that this order is a commanding order, that it gives the power to Mr. Halilovic of commanding the operation, which is a totally misleading impression, in our submission. And as pointed out earlier, the Defence has made a request to obtain the chain of custody of that document and also asked the Prosecution for information as to the person who translated that document. The Defence thinks it is perhaps the -- the point to raise again or to point Your Honours, at least, to a filing from the Defence from the 16th of August, 2004 where the Defence made a number of pretty serious allegations against a Prosecution investigator which -- who has been named on a number of occasion this is week. And Your Honour will be familiar with that person. We think that the issue is one which is much more than an issue of language, and I draw the Chamber's attention to this filing so that the matter can be decided further. But in relation to that issue, and before the Trial Chamber takes any decision on that matter, the Defence believe that we are entitled to obtain the chain of custody of that document, an explanation as to who translated that document, and what happened with that document. Concerning the second issue, which is the issue of the swapping, if I may use that expression, of the old version to the new version. There's been what we could call a tour de passe-passe between the document. The document which was part of the Rule 65 ter and which had been given to the Defence was the old version and only, I think, during the testimony of Mr. Gusic did the Defence realise that another document had replaced this document. And neither the Defence nor the Trial Chamber had been given any notice that an exhibit has been swapped for another. This is a totally new document that Your Honour have seen and this is not the document upon which we based ourself or that the -- the Confirming Judge based itself or that, for that matter, the military expert of the Prosecution based itself. And I think that the Defence and the Trial Chamber are entitled to an explanation as to what happened and the circumstances under which an exhibit was replaced by another. These are our submissions, Your Honour, in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, this document is a very important document to this case. And as for the document submitted to the Confirming Judge, I have to say that I myself have been or am now a Confirming Judge to some cases. I don't think that Confirming Judge will base her finding entirely on one piece of document to confirm an indictment. There must be a lot of supporting material for her consideration as well as there may be some conference between the Prosecution and the Confirming Judge concerning with the clarification on certain points in the indictment. And the Defence also said this document, the command document, was shown to some witnesses, but I believe that most of the witnesses who understand the B/C/S will read the original one instead of the translations at all. Only we, the international persons, who could possibly be misled by this document. It seems to me that the Defence failed to show any prejudice against their interest in this concerning with the document, and they did not request any remedies to that aspect. But anyway, we'll take into consideration of the submissions of the both parties when we consider the admission of that document or maybe we could find another time at a later stage when there are more informations available to reconsider this issue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just so that it's -- that we make our point quite clear here. We were not asking for the exclusion of the document as retranslated or as properly translated by CLSS. In addition, the Defence fully agrees with Your Honour about the process of confirmation of an indictment. The Defence would like to underline, however, that this is the document in this case. This is the most fundamental document. In addition, this document has polluted a number of other witnesses who don't speak the B/C/S language, such as the military expert, who in turn submitted a report to the Confirming Judge based on the order in question. The other thing which the Defence would like to point out at this stage and in relation to Your Honour's statement, is that the Defence has raised a number of very, very grave concerns about other material which was put before the Confirming Judge at the time, including many, many witnesses' statements who the Defence thinks might have been tampered with. These issues have been raised in several filings, in particular the filing which I referred to of the 16th of August, 2004. Your Honour have -- has heard this week evidence to that effect from at least two witnesses. What we would like is -- or what we are seeking at this stage is not to exclude the document of the 30th of August as properly translated but for an explanation on the part of the Prosecution and an order to that effect to explain what went on, what happened, both in relation to the original document and in relation to the swapping of that document. And the Defence believe, with respect, that we are entitled to such a remedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, so you are in agreement that we admit one document, that is, the latest document with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- with the memo as an annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can assist the Chamber. There is one explanation, that is, when our expert was given the document, it was not the document -- the old one, it was the -- the newly translated one which he got. In fact, that was what prompted the new translation was when we were -- we were supposed to give the document to the expert. And so the only person- and I do agree with the Defence to the extent that it was the Defence -- it was the Confirming Judge which got the old translation which we have now withdrawn. But the expert did not. Perhaps it may assist if I give a short explanation, Your Honours, with your leave, as to how we came upon these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the -- the best way is that you submit a memo to the Chamber or to the Defence team on that very issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have actually verbally explained to the Defence as to what exactly happened, and I -- and I have all the -- the pieces of paper which sort of deal with our documents and how they come into the collection, et cetera, but I would be very happy to do a memo. And I think we have also in some letters explained this to them. But if it will assist, we are very happy to do a new memo to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just one point, Your Honour. If the position of the Prosecution is correct in relation to the document which was given to the military expert, we would like to point out that the report of that expert was done, if I believe, sometime in June 2002, and we are quite concerned that it took the Prosecution almost two years to give us the translation of the actual document. And our understanding is that Major General Ridgway, the expert, in fact received the old document. We're not questioning the truth of what has just been told to us but we think that this issue should be addressed in the memo that the Prosecution will submit to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I believe so. I believe that the Prosecution will mention that issue in her memo. Let's go to -- go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. And I said good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Mettraux: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sakrak.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back where I left you last night. You were telling the Trial Chamber about your arrival in Grabovica and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, asking the troops to go and accommodate themselves into empty houses. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having given that order, Celo then promptly left Grabovica; isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And only after Celo had left did someone from the 9th Brigade look for alternative accommodation; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your evidence is also that in fact you don't know why this person decided to look for accommodation, whether it was because the house was -- the houses were too small or simply because they didn't find them comfortable enough; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you know, however, is that Nihad Vlahovljak ordered all of you from his platoon to go and find accommodation with local civilians.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just passed on the message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no one before him had suggested to you that you would be accommodated with local civilians.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the first time anyone made such a suggestion to you, the first time that people said that you should or that you would be accommodated with local civilians.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't go to be accommodated with local civilians of your own free will. You did because Nihad told you so.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. "Of your own free will" implies something involuntary. Military is of course subject to a form of discipline and hierarchy. An order -- being issued with an order and a bang, doesn't imply that you're doing it of your own free will because if you're in the army, you're subjected to certain disciplinary measures. I'd just ask my friend to put it in a proper form. If he means "involuntary," say so. If he means "you were ordered to do so," say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I -- in this occasion, I see no difference with the "free will" or "voluntarily." But if the Prosecution prefers like this, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We believe the question was clear enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that the answer was clear enough from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it -- from the Prosecution's perspective, it's not. Is the witness replying that it was involuntary, he was forced to do something? Or is he replying to a question which he understands to mean, "I was ordered to do it and because I was in the army, I obeyed an order"? There is quite a difference. One is you could be forced. It could be at gunpoint. You could have been marched there. The other is, "I was ordered to do so, so I just went around the village looking." It's entirely unclear from that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the situation in this case is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakrak, you had nothing against Croats. As a matter of fact, you had many Croatian friends. Did you hear me, Mr. Sakrak?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your answer is yes, you had Croatian friends and you had nothing against Croats?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing against Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also indicated in evidence in chief that at first Pero Maric was not particularly happy to see you arrive with your colleagues and that at first he didn't want you to enter his home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you eventually persuaded him to let you in and let you sleep in two rooms in his house; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you didn't use nor did any of your colleagues use any threats or force to persuade him to let you in his home.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody applied any force. He agreed to it himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to finish this issue of accommodation, sir. Did you at any time or, rather, on that night, on the 8th, between the 8th and the 9th of September, 1993, did you see anyone sleeping outside in the meadows or in front of houses?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Because we find it hard to hear the witness. He has to open his mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Sakrak, to move a bit forward. The interpreters have problems hearing your voice. Am I correct in understanding your answer as a "no," to the effect that no, you didn't see anyone sleeping outside in the night between the 8th or the 9th of September, 1993 either in front of houses or in meadows? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody slept inside houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to ask you a few questions about the atmosphere, so to say, in the village when you arrived. As far as the soldiers were concerned, you, the 9th Brigade, when you arrived, the atmosphere was quite euphoric, wasn't it? People were happy to be there.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were glad to be finally outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of the members of the 9th Brigade demonstrated loudly their happiness by shooting in the air as they arrived.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Everybody expresses happiness in a variety of ways. I personally would not regard shooting in the air as an incident because it was not targeting anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of the locals greeted you in a very friendly manner. Some of the locals cooked food for you and others offered you drinks, like Pero did.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of -- some of the members of your brigade just went on to pick up fruit in the village, figs. It was the season of the figs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Others went fishing and others still went swimming as they arrived in the village.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until the incident that you've described yesterday, the incident involving Pero Maric, there had been no problems with the locals.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no problems. The atmosphere was a friendly one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was no reason to believe until the Pero Maric incident that something bad would happen.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sakrak. I will repeat it. Until the -- we will come to the -- to the timing, but until the incident involving Pero Maric, you had no reason to believe that something bad would happen, something of the sort which eventually happened in the village.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had no reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, as far as you, Mr. Sakrak, can tell, the murder of Pero Maric was the first incident of that sort to occur in Grabovica on that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the evidence which you've given to the Chamber yesterday, the murder of Pero Maric must have taken place at around 8.00 in the evening of the 8th of September, 1993? Would that be correct, sir, or approximately correct? Or if you can specify it more clearly, please do so.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was toward dusk. I can't say it was 8.00 precisely. But as the days were getting longer, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And there was no combat activity in the village on that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pero Maric was not in any way engaged in any military activity on that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that earlier that day you said, I believe, 3.00, 3.30, there had been a bit of taunting and verbal abuse towards -- directed towards Pero Maric because someone in your brigade had found a picture of his son in HVO uniform.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But by the time Pero -- I'm sorry, by the time Musa Hota arrived at dusk, the situation had calmed down and you and the other people who were sleeping in this house were actually sitting around the table and having drinks with Pero Maric; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated that a number of -- other than the soldiers who slept in this house - and you said that there were about seven or eight of them - other than those soldiers, a number of individuals came to the house on that night, on the night of the 8th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came and went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one or two such individuals or individual came together with Musa Hota; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, who that individual or those two individuals were?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you their first and last names. I can only guess or assume, but I don't want to mention names because I'm not sure who was with him. I know Musa arrived with some other people, but I couldn't tell you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can we go in private session for a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the killing of Pero Maric - so that we're all clear about this issue - had nothing to do with military combat.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It had even less to do with the mission which you were sent to perform in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this incident, you've indicated that you and your friends went to sleep -- went to sleep, and that the next morning - that would be the 9th of September - you woke up in Pero Maric's house.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you woke up on the 9th of September, you had no idea that you would be involved in the killing of civilians during that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't assume something like that might happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you had the slightest indication that this could be the case, you would have done everything in your power to avoid having a part therein; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you went out that morning, you said at around 9.00 or 9.30, the order which you received from Nihad was totally unexpected.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you hadn't drank any alcohol that morning nor had you taken any drugs, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't use either alcohol or drugs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nor, as far as you can tell, had Sead Karagic or Haris Rajkic, your two friends.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just like me, no, they hadn't taken anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also mentioned a lineup organised by Celo on the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date, but there was a line-up when we were supposed to go to Dreznica, a line-up in which I participated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the line-up, sir, took place on the day after the killing had taken place in Grabovica, of the Zadros, that is. I mean, the day after you killed two members of the Zadro family. That was the next day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line-up in which I participated was several days later, before we left for Dreznica. I heard there was another line-up on the same day when the boys were found and that was a line-up in which I did not participate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is because from the time when you heard that the boys had been found, you did everything to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you were hiding from Celo.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he would have punished us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also talked about another incident involving or allegedly involving Mr. Habib.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This incident, sir, if it happened at all, and according to Mr. Habib's own words to you, would have happened around 1.00 p.m. on the 9th of September, 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know nor did you mention the name or identity of the person which Mr. Habib allegedly killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. He didn't mention the name at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't even know, sir, whether that person was a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know if it's true. Maybe he just said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't see him take that person away, did you?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. He just told me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you just pointed out to this court, it may just have been an invention or some sort of stupid boasting on the part of Mr. Habib.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but a shot was heard. That doesn't mean that the shot was aimed at that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the shot was only heard in the general direction of the house where Mr. Habib said he committed that crime.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that house was a couple of hundred metres from where you were at the time when you heard the shot.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the killing, sir, of the Zadro family, that killing, sir, took place around 12.00 or 13.00 on the 9th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the killing of that family took place at a time when the killing in the village had almost finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this -- is this something this witness knows? There's a proper way of establishing the foundation for this particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I certainly will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, sir, of the 15th of December, 2003 given to the Office of the Prosecution at page 7 of your statement you indicated that at the time when this incident occurred, the killing in the village had - and I quote your words in the English translation - "almost finished." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shooting in the village was indeed abating and it soon ceased altogether.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it -- it ceased altogether, and I quote again your words from the same statement, this time paragraph 30: "It stopped altogether in early afternoon."

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you can tell, sir, after noon or perhaps shortly thereafter the killing had stopped in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, is this -- it appears to be speculation, from the Prosecution's perspective. The witness can give evidence of what he saw, told, or was heard. He can't be asked to speculate about what might have happened that he didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that's because, you know, the previous statement of this witness. Because the witness testified it stopped altogether in early afternoon, and the Defence counsel is entitled to make a clarification or ask further questions along this line. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as far as you can tell with your own eyes and your own ears, the killing had stopped in early afternoon of the 9th of September, 1993; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, sir, you made your way back from the Zadros house to Pero Maric's house where you were staying and you came back with Sead and Haris; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you -- and as you reached this house, you came across Nihad. It was immediately after you had come back, so it must have been shortly after noon, shortly after 12.00 on the 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, Nihad conveyed an order to you to bury the bodies of the victims.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little after that. Not right away, but a little while after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would have been less than half an hour later, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as he gave you the order, that is, Nihad, he knew very well that what he was asking of you was illegal?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nihad didn't issue the order. He only transmitted it. As to whether he knew it was illegal or not, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nihad told you, as you just pointed out, that an order had come from Vehbija Karic to clean up traces of crimes because he said they suspected that the UNPROFOR was coming in the village.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you, sir, did not verify whether Nihad had really received such an order from Karic.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I will -- I will try to formulate it a bit better. You were not in a position at the time to determine whether Nihad really had received such an order from Karic or whether perhaps he was deceiving you in that regard to give more authority to the order which he was giving you.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't check it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that it's clear, I'm not criticising you or anything or questioning what you -- what you're saying. I'm just trying to determine the facts. Because you had no way yourself to ascertain whether Nihad had indeed received that order or that alleged order from Karic.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not telling this Trial Chamber that Karic actually gave that order. All you're saying is that Nihad claimed to have received such an order.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the actual cleaning-up of the scene, as soon as you had received this order, passed on, conveyed, or given by Nihad, you immediately set up with Haris, Sead, and two others to bury bodies.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was all done in the greatest hurry because you were concerned that the UNPROFOR was indeed trying to -- or might come in the village.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that by mid-afternoon on the 9th of September, 1993, and again, as far as you can tell from your own eyes or ears, there were no more traces of crimes in the village of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no more traces, at least none that I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you could see or as far as you can tell this Court, all the bodies of the victims had been buried in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw no trucks coming in the village on that day, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor, as a matter of fact, did you see UNPROFOR trying to enter the village.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just one question about evidence which you gave -- or several questions, as a matter of fact, which you gave to the Prosecution about what happened on that day. You said that you could not see or you did not see anyone trying to enter the village on that day. Am I correct in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the answer, Mr. Sakrak. The interpreters did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know, sir, whether anyone tried to enter the village. You don't know that.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I agree with you fully. Because I didn't walk around much. If I didn't see that, it doesn't mean other people didn't see it or that they didn't arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, actually, after the incident in which you took part - and I mean the killing of the Zadro family - you mostly stayed in or just outside the house of Pero Maric. You didn't go around the village, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never heard that the Minister of Interior, Mr. Bakir Alispahic, ever tried to enter the village of Grabovica on the 9th or the 10th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day after the incident in which you took part, the killing of the Zadros, most of the troops which had been accommodated in the village left Grabovica for combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the individuals involved in the killing of civilians in Grabovica, other than yourself, Haris Rajkic, Sead Karagic, and as far as Pero Maric is concerned, you don't know who else committed crimes in Grabovica - and by "crimes" I mean murders - you don't know the names of those persons.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know either, sir, whether the individuals whom you saw walking around the village as you were going towards the house of the Zadros themselves had any part in the killing of civilians in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I will try to -- to rephrase it. You've indicated yesterday that as you walked towards -- as you walked away from Pero's house, you came across a number of soldiers, one of whom or several of whom told you that "everything is clear down there." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, sir: You don't know whether any of those individuals whom you passed or met or saw on that day took any part in the killing of civilians in Grabovica on that day. You don't know that, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the victims, sir, of the incident in Grabovica, you don't know and you're unable to ascertain or to give any evidence to this Trial Chamber as to how many people might have been killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor can you assist the Court in any way in relation to the identity of those people, other than Pero Maric and his wife, and you've indicated obviously the Zadro family. Other than those people, sir, you cannot assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor can you give any additional evidence than the one you've already given about the circumstances in which other civilians - and I mean other than the Zadros and the Maric, Pero and Dragica - might have been killed. You cannot give any other evidence about that -- about the circumstances of the death of other individuals.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about Pero and the Zadro family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated yesterday that you were a mere foot soldier in the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, you were not aware or you were not privy to the structure of the operation or the commanding structure of the operation in which you were taking a part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer, sir, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday, sir, you've indicated in response to a question by the Prosecution that Sefer Halilovic might have been in charge of the operation. This is what you told the Prosecution yesterday, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But those are only assumptions, because nothing was formally said as to Mr. Sefer Halilovic leading that operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I put a proposition to you in that regard. Would I be correct in suggesting that your assumption as to the role and function of Mr. Halilovic during that operation is based on two things: Firstly, you thought that at the time Mr. Halilovic was still the commander of the Bosnian army; and, secondly, that considering the size and the importance of the operation, a very senior official or officer of the army must be in charge of that operation? Isn't that the basis for your assumption, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, just that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you just indicated, you never saw any document suggesting that Mr. Halilovic had been given such a role.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did I see any documents, nor did I see Mr. Sefer himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see Sefer Halilovic in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him before or after. I mean, I didn't see Mr. Sefer Halilovic a single time in the period I spent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've indicated yesterday as well to the Prosecution that until the year 2000, I believe, you had not been interviewed by anyone about the incidents in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's quite normal, sir, because considering what you had done down there in Grabovica, you were very careful not to let anyone know that you had been in Grabovica at the time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was no list, sir, of the individuals, the members of the 9th Brigade, who had gone to Herzegovina. There was no search list. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, unless my learned friend can establish how this witness who he has just obtained evidence from was a mere "foot soldier" would be in a position to know what sort of list or records the ABiH kept of soldiers and where they were, he can't ask this question. He has to -- there's a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will rephrase, Your Honour. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you shown a list of the individuals who were to be taken in Grabovica either before you went there or upon your return? Did you see such a list?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you returned to Sarajevo, you were very careful, sir, to distance yourself from many of the members of the 9th Brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, you stayed away as much as you could from Nihad Vlahovljak; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not turn yourself to the police, neither did you volunteer to give a statement at the time about what happened; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for several years, sir, you denied having had any part in what happened in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any individuals who were directly involved in the killing in Grabovica in September 1993, you acknowledged your responsibility instead of inventing intricate stories to explain yourself out of the -- out of the events. Isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. First of all, my learned friend has to establish that the witness knows who the other people involved in the killings were, what stories they would have invented, who they told them to, whether they were given to the authorities, whether this prevented the authorities from investigating and so on. He can certainly confine it to what's in this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well -- the story referring to Your Honour, the -- he gave a statement, or a suspect interview, to be more precise, in the year 2000 to the Prosecution where he himself acknowledged yesterday that he had invented a story. I was referring to the story of that witness, who invented a story and who told it to the Prosecution. I will move on, Your Honour, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after your return to Sarajevo, many members of the 9th Brigade were arrested and detained as part of an operation known as "Trebevic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself were not arrested, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, because in my military service book that we had to produce during a rest, it was not recorded that I was a member of the 9th Brigade in 1993/1994. Something else was written in my military service book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the back of the document which I showed you yesterday, sir, to the effect that you only formally became a member of the 9th Brigade on the 30th November, 1993; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, however, that a number of other members of the 9th Brigade were arrested during that operation and that several of them were interviewed about the incident in Grabovica. You know that.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for certain. That is perfectly true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know, sir, that none of them was charged with committing a crime in relation to Grabovica; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean was any of them indicted? Is that what you ask? I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put it in another way. Of all the members of the 9th Brigade who were arrested during the Trebevic operation, none of them was indicted in relation to a crime related to Grabovica. I'm not talking about other incidents in -- to which they might have been referred, but none of them, as far as you know, or perhaps with the exception of Musa Hota, were charged with anything in relation to Grabovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know for a fact, sir, that Sefer Halilovic was arrested as part of the same operation.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know, sir, that Sefer Halilovic was detained for more than three weeks during that operation; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But whereas Mr. Halilovic was removed from the army on the 1st of November, 1993, all of the former members of the 9th Brigade continued to act as soldiers in the Bosnian army; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of the former members of the 9th Brigade, just as you did, joined the 105th Brigade, that's the 105 Brigade. Isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would concern, for instance, individuals such as yourself, Haris Rajkic, Sead Karagic, Sabahudin Djenanovic [phoen], known as Dziki, and that also involves Nihad and Celo; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, just to finish up a short question. I believe that you were gravely wounded in 1994. Is that correct, sir? Was it in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you left the army because you had been gravely wounded and couldn't continue as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for a while you decided to go back to studies and you went to university to study criminology; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for some reason you stopped your studies and went to work for the OSCE instead for a little while; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: OSC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't stay there for very long. After that, sir, you found another job with the Commission on the Establishment of War Crimes in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was demobilised, I started working. I worked for about two months perhaps in the Commission for the Investigation of War Crimes and then I transferred to the OSC, to which the commission was affiliated.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That would be all the questions from the Defence. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Sakrak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's high time to take a break, and we'll have 30 minutes' break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the break, I was approached by the Prosecutor and provided with information that's directly relevant -- yes, I'm sorry, I'm reminded now that we should go into the private session, and I ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re, your redirect, please. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Defence counsel Mr. Mettraux, asked you, Mr. Sakrak, about the membership or the ethnic composition of the 9th Motorised Brigade. Were there any Serbs or Croats to your knowledge in the group of soldiers who went from Sarajevo to Grabovica in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the Serb or Croat members of the 9th Brigade participated in the murder of the Croat villagers in that killing spree on the 9th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the presence or otherwise of groups -- military groups called Cedo's Wolves or the Handzar Division. You said you didn't know if they were there. Did you know of their existence when you were in Grabovica in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that they existed or that they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have known what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know who belongs to what unit. I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence was that you joined the 9th Motorised Brigade sometime shortly before you left for Herzegovina in September 1993. Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the Faculty of Physical Education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where's that?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that army barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The Defence has asked no question about the location of the 9th Brigade or the facilities in which they were staying. I can't see how this could ever come out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you asked the time that the witness joined the 9th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I asked about the timing. But certainly nothing to do with their location or the facilities which they were using in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re, unless this question is closely related to the cross-examination, I don't hope ask you to expand the scope of the redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't know whether this kind of evidence is relevant to our present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submission, the relevance is this: In cross-examination and through the tender of that document showing that the witness formally joined the 9th Brigade in November 1993, there seemed to be a suggestion or it seems to be the Defence case that he was not really a part of the 9th Motorised Brigade before November 1993 and, therefore, it would have been impossible for the Bosnian authorities, had they so wished to track him down, because he wasn't listed as being in the 9th Brigade. Now, I'm asking him about where he was located, who he was there with, was it 9th Brigade -- Mountain Brigade -- Motorised Brigade premises, just to establish in re-examination that he was in fact in the 9th Brigade and locatable in that -- in the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that we come across an issue of de jure or de facto soldiers, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, in effect, the way the Defence case on that point has been presented by the Prosecution is inaccurate, Your Honour. We are not suggesting that Mr. Sakrak was in fact a member of the 9th Brigade from the period from September to November 1993. What we are saying is he joined three or four days before going to Herzegovina, remained a member of that brigade during the period between September and November, but only became a member formally on the 30th of November. That's the only thing the Defence is suggesting at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I think this issue is settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown, Mr. Sakrak, a copy of some records from the 9th Motorised Brigade suggesting that you formally joined in November 1993. Did your own -- I just can't think of the word -- military registration book, what did it say about your military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has already answered that question in relation to his arrest. He's indicated to the Court that the reason why he wasn't arrested is precisely because of that, because his military record did not indicate that he was a member of the 9th Brigade at the time. This question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about what his own registration book says, and I'm going to ask him about investigations which arise from that. And I'm not quite sure it was answered in the way my friend suggests that he wasn't arrested because he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have the right to make any clarifications on that issue. But only this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your military -- your own registration book, the one -- the record you kept yourself, what did it say about when you formally joined the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned from Herzegovina, did you go back to the same place, that is, the Faculty of Physical Education?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I know what the objection is going to be, and I can answer it. It is directly relevant to the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the important question, Your Honour, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just finish, please. I understand -- I anticipate the objection. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to be anticipated on this matter, Your Honour. It's for me to make the objection, and the objection is, again, that this matter has not been raised in cross-examination. It's been raised before. It's raised again. And this has not been raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have already made a ruling that this issue has been settled. There's no disputes between the parties concerning of that particular issue, so you may skip that over, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not the issue I'm after. There seems -- maybe there's a misunderstanding or maybe I'm not expressing myself as clearly as I should. The issue I'm attempting to clarify was the possibility of the witness being investigated or arrested upon his return from - if I can finish, please - from Herzegovina. Now, Mr. Mettraux just said he wasn't arrested because he wasn't on the books. All I want from the witness is where he was, was he with the other soldiers, the same ones he returned with, from Grabovica, the ones who were interrogated in October 1993. Was he with them at the same time; that is, was he physically able to be interrogated. And that -- in my submission, that must rise out of cross-examination because Mr. Mettraux just put to Your Honours the suggestion that he wasn't arrested because he wasn't formally written down in the books. I must be entitled to clarify that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, there's no clarification to be brought to this issue. There was no cross-examination in relation to the investigation of Mr. Sakrak. The only issue which was raised at the time was the issue as to whether or not he had been arrested. That's the only one issue that was raised in relation to this matter. There was no issue going to the issue of investigation which Mr. Re is now trying to lead in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, you may ask a direct leading question to this witness concerning of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: His own arrest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He wasn't arrested till 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe why not he was arrested during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993 - and the Defence has just conceded that you were a member of the 9th Brigade between September and November - did you consider yourself subject to order and discipline of the 9th Mountain Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just a second. Could the Prosecution be more precise about whether he considered himself. He stated the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I actually didn't finish the question. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question is not direct enough. I allowed you to make a very direct and leading question to the witness, just up to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe if I could return to that. I've got a different area I wish to -- to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence asked you in cross-examination, Mr. Sakrak, whether you had seen Mr. Sefer Halilovic in Grabovica when you were there. Did you know Mr. Halilovic personally at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him through the media, but I never saw him down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you knew him through the media, are you saying you knew what he looked like? You'd seen him in the media?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew very well what he looked like, and I could not make a mistake. I assert with full responsibility that Mr. Sefer Halilovic was not there, at least as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the first things Mr. Mettraux asked you today was about when you went looking for accommodation, and the question was: Was it not of your own free will? And you answered "yes." I want you to clarify what you meant by that. Did you mean by the answer "yes" to the question "was it not of your own free will," that you were forced or that you were obeying an order to look for accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question, but from what I understand, is that we were told or the suggestion was made to go looking elsewhere, other than in those two houses. Whether it was an order or not, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify what you meant when you responded to the question "it was not of your own free will." What -- what did you understand the question, when it was asked, in the sense of -- you were doing something not of your own free will -- what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was also suggested to you that Habib Alic was boasting about having raped and killed a woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it wasn't suggested. What was put to the witness is an alternative as to whether Mr. Sakrak would give evidence as to whether this event happened or whether it was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was suggested to you in cross-examination that Mr. Habib Alic was possibly boasting about having killed and raped a woman. In your experience, as a person, have you ever heard anyone else boast about having possibly killed and raped a woman? Has anyone ever boasted to you before about killing and raping a woman?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have to object again. This is totally speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you on that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 9th of September, Mr. Sakrak, after you participated in the murder of the Zadro family, where -- where did you go after the incident you described with Mr. Habib Alic telling you about having attempted to rape and then killing a woman? Where did you spend the rest of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it does arise directly out of cross-examination, with respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Where did you spend the right of the afternoon before nightfall? Were you in the house? Were you walking around? Were you in the village? Were you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ENES SAKRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was inside the house or around the house. Never too far away from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the other houses in the village on the afternoon of the 9th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. I object again, Your Honour. There was no evidence led in cross-examination in relation to his whereabouts during the afternoon. He was asked where he was. He said, "In the house or around the house." That is all that was asked. The question has been asked again by the Prosecution in re-examination. There was nothing in cross-examination about him visiting other houses or such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, I believe that the witness has answered your question already. He said he was "inside the house or around the house. Never too far away from the house."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So your next question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do accept that. And I do accept that it was slightly repetitive and it goes directly to the issue of what else he could have seen that afternoon, which was directly covered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand the lines of your question, but I think your question has been answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you -- when Mr. Mettraux questioned you and you answered him about your belief that there were no more killings that afternoon, were you in a position from being inside the house or just slightly around the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please don't -- can you please let me finish the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I have an objection, Your Honour, in relation to this matter. The Defence should not be misquoted. The witness was not asked to express a belief.
